title: The parts of a sentence a writer works with

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A sentence is built from clauses. A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. A subordinate clause also has a subject and a verb, but it cannot stand alone. Words such as although, because, even if, when, since or while open one.

The verb expresses an action, an occurrence or a state of being. A verb may carry a small word with it, as in “left out”; the two together are the verb.

The subject names what the clause is about: the thing the verb is said of. Its main word is the noun the verb is said of, and the rest of the phrase describes that noun.

The object is the noun that receives the action of the verb.

The doer is whoever or whatever performs the action, whether or not it is the subject.

Voice says which of them is the subject. In the active voice, the subject performs the action of the verb. In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: the active sentence’s object becomes the subject. The doer moves into a phrase beginning “by”, or is left out. A passive verb has a form of “to be” and a past participle, the form that follows “has” or “was”: measured, given, left.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
The verb is the word for what happens: measured, rose, is.

Ask “who or what” in front of the verb: who measured? The answer is the subject.

In “We measured the weight”, the doer is “we”, and “we” is also the subject. That is the active voice.

Turn it round: “The weight was measured”. Now the thing measured is the subject, and the doer has gone. That is the passive voice. Its sign is a form of “to be” with a verb ending, usually, in -ed.

A main clause can stand as a sentence on its own. A clause that starts with “because”, “when” or “although” cannot.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Take a sentence of the kind found in the methods chapter of almost any thesis. This one is made up.

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants by the investigator before the interview.

Find the verb first. Ask what happens in the sentence: something was obtained. The verb is “was obtained”. It carries both signs of the passive: a form of “to be”, “was”, and a past participle, “obtained”.

Now find the subject. Ask what was obtained: written informed consent. That is the subject, and it is not the doer. Consent did nothing. It received the action.

Now find the doer. Look for “by”. The investigator obtained the consent.

Turn the sentence round so that the doer is the subject.

The investigator obtained written informed consent from all participants before the interview.

The subject is now “the investigator”, the verb is “obtained”, and the object is “written informed consent”. The facts have not changed. Neither has the tense: both sentences are in the past. Only the voice has changed.

Now try a harder one, from the same made-up chapter.

Data were collected using a pretested questionnaire and entered in a spreadsheet.

The verbs are “were collected” and “(were) entered”. Both are passive. Look for “by”. There is none. The sentence never says who collected the data, or who typed them in. To turn it into the active voice, you have to know the answer. “Two trained interviewers collected the data” is a different sentence from “I collected the data”, and a reader judging the study needs to know which one is true. The passive let the writer skip that question. The reader cannot skip it.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The two signs of the passive are a test, not a proof. The guideline that lists them says both may not appear in every passive sentence. “The forms got lost” is passive with no form of “to be”. And “the clinic was closed on Sunday” may describe how the clinic was, not something anybody did to it. When the signs mislead, ask the plain question: did the subject do the action, or receive it?

Turning a sentence into the active voice is a test you can run, not an order to obey. Some passive sentences are the better sentence. The next section shows when.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
The subject is not always one word. Read this sentence. It is made up, but its figure is the survey’s own.

In the fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), the proportion of women aged 15 to 49 in India who had overweight or obesity was 24.0 per cent.

First take off any opening phrase that ends with a comma: “In the fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)”. Then find the verb. It is “was”.

Ask what was 24.0 per cent. The answer is the whole of “the proportion of women aged 15 to 49 in India who had overweight or obesity”. That long phrase is the subject. Its main word is “proportion”. The rest tells you which proportion.

Count the words between “proportion” and “was”. There are 13. The reader holds all 13 in mind while waiting for the verb. The next section calls this the gap between subject and verb, and asks you to close it.

Inside that subject sits a clause of its own: “who had overweight or obesity”. It opens with “who”, a word the list above does not name. It has a subject, “who”, and a verb, “had”. Read it alone and it is not a sentence. So it is a subordinate clause.

Now a sentence with two clauses side by side.

Because the fact sheet’s adult rows cover ages 15 to 49 only, they say nothing about women of 50 or older.

Read each clause alone. “They say nothing about women of 50 or older” stands as a sentence: it is the main clause. “Because the fact sheet’s adult rows cover ages 15 to 49 only” does not stand: it is subordinate. The main point of the sentence belongs in the main clause, and here it is.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
“Take off the opening phrase, then find the verb” works for most sentences in a paper. It fails on a question (“Did the proportion rise?”), where the verb comes first, and on a sentence that starts “There were”, where “there” only fills the place of the subject. In “There were three villages without a road”, the subject is “villages”.

The count of 13 words is for this one sentence. It shows what a long subject costs. It is not a limit.

points.html: “The passive voice is the past tense” is the error. Voice says whether the subject did the action or received it. Tense says when. When an editor tells you to remove the passive, check voice, not tense.
Verb first. Then ask “who or what” in front of it to find the subject. Then look for “by”, or ask who did it, to find the doer.
A passive sentence with no “by” hides who did the work. Before you submit, find each passive verb and ask whether the reader needs the doer. If yes, name it.
The two signs of the passive, a form of “to be” and an -ed word, are a quick test that can mislead. When the test is unsure, ask whether the subject did the action or received it.
Put the point of a sentence in its main clause. If your finding sits in the subordinate clause, the reader will weigh it less than you meant.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “The passive hides the doer, so every passive sentence is wrong and must go.” It does not follow. A passive sentence is right when the doer does not matter, or when the paragraph is telling the story of the thing acted on. Gopen and Swan’s example is “Pollen is dispersed by bees”, which is the better sentence in a paragraph about pollen. The passive is a choice of subject. The next section shows how to make that choice.

blocks.label: Reporting it
blocks.html: The investigator obtained written informed consent from every participant before the interview.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, name the two signs of a passive verb. Then say what is wrong with the statement “the passive voice is the past tense”, with one example.
blocks.answer:
The first sign is a form of “to be”: is, was, were, has been. The second is a past participle, the form that follows “has” or “was”, which usually ends in -ed. Both may not appear in every passive sentence.

Voice and tense are different things. Voice says whether the subject did the action or received it. Tense says when. “Weight is measured” is passive and present. “We measured weight” is active and past.

blocks.prompt:
The three sentences below are made up. In each one, mark the verb, the subject and its main word, the object if there is one, and the voice. Name the doer, or say that the sentence does not name one. Where there are two clauses, say which is the main clause.

  1. The auxiliary nurse midwife weighed every child at the anganwadi, the government child care centre of the village.
  2. Three villages were left out because the road was closed.
  3. There were many households without a weighing scale.
blocks.answer:
Sentence by sentence:

  1. Verb: “weighed”. Subject: “the auxiliary nurse midwife”, main word “midwife”. Object: “every child”. Active voice. The doer is the subject, the midwife. One clause.

  2. Two clauses. The main clause is “Three villages were left out”. Its verb is “were left out”, its subject “three villages”, main word “villages”. It is passive, and it names no doer: the sentence does not say who left the villages out.

    The subordinate clause is “because the road was closed”. Its subject is “the road” and its verb “was closed”. It may be passive (someone closed the road) or describe how the road was (shut). The sentence does not tell you which.

    A reader judging the survey would want to know who decided to drop the villages.

  3. Verb: “were”. The word “there” stands where a subject usually stands, but it names nothing. Ask what there were: households. The subject is “many households without a weighing scale”, main word “households”. No object, and no action, so no doer and no voice to change. A rewrite gives the sentence a real subject and verb: “Many households had no weighing scale.”

blocks.prompt: Open the manuscript section you chose for this book’s build. Find every passive verb in it. For each one, write down the doer, if you know it. Then mark the ones where a reader judging your work would need to know who did it.
blocks.answer:
There is no single right list, so check your own against three tests.

  • You found the verb first, then the subject, then looked for “by”. A passive with no “by” is the kind most worth marking.
  • For each marked verb, the doer is something a reviewer could ask about. Who measured? Who interviewed? Who entered or cleaned the data? Who decided which participants to leave out?
  • Verbs whose doer does not change the result are left unmarked. “The two readings were averaged” gives the same average whoever did the sum.

If you could not name the doer of a marked verb, that is a gap in your methods, not only in your sentence. Find out, and write it down.
